newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-BARNARD HOPING TO STAY WITH FERRARI.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-BARNARD HOPING TO STAY WITH FERRARI.

text.p: British designer John Barnard, the man who has designed more Ferraris in the last decade than any other, hopes to remain with the team despite the arrival of fellow-Briton Ross Brawn as technical director.

Barnard, whose F310B car was dubbed on Tuesday as "a red Williams" because of its similarities to the Renault-powered car when it was unveiled at the team's launch, denied he was poised to leave the team.

His contract ends this year, but he has started talks already about a new deal -- though he admitted, also, that he would be attracted to a possible new challenge if Frenchman Alain Prost succeeded in buying Ligier to set up a new all-French team.

"I want to stay in Formula One and I would like to continue working with Ferrari," Brawn said. "But I cannot say yet what the future will hold. I would be very interested in working with Alain, but that is altogether another matter.
"For now, I am hoping to form a good relationship with Ross and to work well with him. I think he will be taking some of the weight off my shoulders!"
Many observers expected Brawn's arrival at Ferrari -- he joined the team shortly before Christmas -- as signalling Barnard's departure. But the two could link in a new partnership.
During his two spells with the team over the last 10 years, Barnard has often felt overloaded by the demands of the team.

But he has steadfastly refused to leave England and live in Italy - - a position which, though it ensured he worked with the most skilled engineers and designers at his own base in Surrey, also vexed the team and stretched its internal communications.

Ferrari president Luca di Montezemolo said on Tuesday that Barnard had for a long time been asked to fulfill his own role as designer and head of research and development and also to assist in running the Maranello technical department and the race team at Grands Prix.
"I got roped into the whole operation," admitted Barnard. "Now I am hoping to gain from Ross's arrival. But how Ferrari want us to operate is up to them -- as is the future."

Di Montezemolo said he and Ferrari had waited a long time to find the right man at a high level to take the job of technical director at Maranello and had passed over the chance of appointing a lower level person several times.

Brawn is expected to mastermind the entire technical operation, using Barnard's British-based operation as the design shop for this year at least, and to also work on running the race team. He will coordinate all of Ferrari's racing team from Italy and will live close to the Maranello headquarters.

"My wife is coming out this weekend so that we can go looking for a house nearby," he said. "I must say it is very exciting for me to have a new challenge, but I think it is going to be at least a year or 18 months before I can master the language."
Brawn's arrival at Ferrari reunites him with twice world champion Michael Schumacher, with whom he worked for four years at Benetton winning both his world titles.

"We know each other well and have worked successfully before, but Michael was not the reason I took this job," said Brawn. "I came here because I wanted to take the opportunity. It was as simple as that -- now I am looking forward to working with John (Barnard) and everyone else. I can see plenty of scope already."
